subject: inla to analyse multi-centre survey data

messages.author: f9c6a2087c744460
messages.subject: inla to analyse multi-centre survey data
parts:
Hi,

So I am working on survey gathered in different centres. So far we have trying to use meta-analysis to combine resutls across centres, or alternatively multi-level models (lmer). However as we only have 3 different centres I would prefer to implement a Bayesian solution and I'm interested to use INLA to do this. There are a couple of things that are unclear to me however. Here is a toy example:

library(INLA)
library(MASS)
dat1 <- birthwt

form1 = low ~ 1 + age + factor(smoke) + f(race, model="iid", hyper=pcprior)
r = inla(form1, family = "binomial", data = dat1, verbose=FALSE) 
r$summary.fixed
r$summary.random

So this is typical of the kind of analysis we would like to do. What I'm not clear on is which is the correct model to use - is iid correct for this ? Or rw2? (also I have not yet considered the priors)
I am also wondering about missing predictor data. In the example if some values of age or smoke are missing can INLA cope with that ? So far we have been doing a complete case analysis, alongside an imputed missings analysis (imputation using the mice package).
In the case that I can't deal with missings within INLA, would it be incorrect to apply the inla model on the imputed data ?

Finally - this model allows only an overall effect for smoking - how can I modify it to allow a different effect of smoking per race (or in my real data per centre)

Many thanks,
James

messages.author: f9c6a2087c744460

parts:
Apologies of folks got multiple emails on my query - I did not realise that would happen!

So I think I've figured out alot of this over the weekend through trial and error.
1. I should use the iid model as rw2 would give me a smoothing effect within levels that I don't want (I think).
2. I can include random slopes as follows:

form1 = low ~ 1 + age + factor(smoke) + f(race, smoke, model="iid")

Or a linear mixed effect model like so:

dat1$race.copy <- dat1$race
form1 = low ~ 1 + age + factor(smoke) + f(race, model="iid")  + f(race.copy, smoke)

Please confirm that I'm getting that right.

This leaves me with the missing predictor data. I've read that I can accommodate this by making a joint model of observed and missing data. Unfortunately I've no idea how to actually do that (I cannot find a worked example anywhere).
So suppose I have missing values of the variable smoke - how do I specify a joint model for such data:

nr <- nrow(dat1)
miss.idx <- sample( nr, round(nr/10))
dat1[miss.idx, "smoke"] <- NA

And finally I'm still wondering could I use multiply imputed data from the mice package ?
Many thanks,
James

Hi,
So I have one more question here - simply about model specification.

Suppose I want a mixed effects model for a categorical model - am I correct to think I can implement that via dummy variables ?
For example restating my example model above:

dat1$race.copy <- dat1$race
form1 = low ~ 1 + age + factor(smoke) + f(race, model="iid")  + f(race.copy, smoke)

Suppose instead of a mixed effects of smoke across race, I have a three level categorical called 'categ' with levels 'alpha', 'beta', 'gamma' and I wish to model mixed effects of this categorical.
Am I correct to specify the model as follows:

dat1$alpha <- ifelse(data1$categ=="alpha", 1, 0)
dat1$beta <- ifelse(data1$categ=="beta", 1, 0)
dat1$gamma <- ifelse(data1$categ=="gamma", 1, 0)


dat1$race.copy1 <- dat1$race
dat1$race.copy2 <- dat1$race
dat1$race.copy3 <- dat1$race


form1 = low ~ 1 + age + alpha + beta + gamma + f(race, model="iid") + f(race.copy1, alpha) + f(race.copy2, beta) + f(race.copy3, gamma)

I wondering have I too many terms here as it looks quite long!

Many thanks in advance,

> form1 = low ~ 1 + age + factor(smoke) + f(race, model="iid")  +
> f(race.copy, smoke)

this should be correct. note that you have a slight confounding with
the 'race' and the 'intercept'.  you can remove this using f(race,
constr=TRUE) to force this effect to sum to zero over 'race', but you
dont have to or even want to)

> Suppose instead of a mixed effects of smoke across race, I have a
> three level categorical called 'categ' with levels 'alpha', 'beta',
> 'gamma' and I wish to model mixed effects of this categorical.
> Am I correct to specify the model as follows:
>
> dat1$alpha <- ifelse(data1$categ=="alpha", 1, 0)
> dat1$beta <- ifelse(data1$categ=="beta", 1, 0)
> dat1$gamma <- ifelse(data1$categ=="gamma", 1, 0)
>
>
> dat1$race.copy1 <- dat1$race
> dat1$race.copy2 <- dat1$race
> dat1$race.copy3 <- dat1$race
>
>
> form1 = low ~ 1 + age + alpha + beta + gamma + f(race, model="iid") +
> f(race.copy1, alpha) + f(race.copy2, beta) + f(race.copy3, gamma)

I think so, yes. note that the precisions are all different in the four
f() models, and if some of them are the same, you can take advantage of
that.
